newsitem.title: USA: Great Providence barrels into beer field.
newsitem.headline: Great Providence barrels into beer field.

text.p: Although he has yet to sell his first glass of beer, Fred Argilagos is confident that his Great Providence Brewing Co. will soon be the toast of New England's increasingly crowded craft brewing industry.
The Waterford, Conn.-based company this week launched a public offering of 1.5 million shares priced at $1.85 each, with a minimum purchase of 200 shares.
It is building a brewery in Providence, R.I., to be ready in mid-1997, with the $2.7 million it intends to raise through the share offering, Argilagos said in an interview.
Argilagos, the founder of the company, projects sales of $12.5 million a year when the brewery hits its maximum annual capacity of 50,000 barrels in a few years.
But for its first year, Great Providence will brew 12,000 barrels, a drop in the bucket compared with Boston Beer Co.'s 900,000 barrels of Samuel Adams beer.
Argilagos is upbeat despite analysts' warnings of a sobering slowdown in the trendy craft beer industry.
"We have 18 million people living within a three-hour drive, so we'll be able to reach our capacity easily," he said.

He sees the glass as half full, arguing that craft beers account for only 2.5 percent of beer sales in New England, compared with 17 percent in the Pacific Northwest. "There's a lot of room for growth here."
But Argilagos concedes that craft beers have disappointed investors who snapped up stock sold in a spree of offerings over the past two years.
Sam Adams is trading at under $10 a share, down from $24 a year ago, and Seattle-based Redhook Ale Brewery Inc. is also under $10, compared with $26 a year ago.
Trade magazine Beer Marketer's Insights projects volume growth of craft beers to slow to 25 percent in 1997, compared with 35-40 percent in 1996.

"The growth is slowing because expectations were too high, and because the competition has increased," said Jennifer Solomon, beverage analyst at Salomon Brothers. "This is a very crowded category," she said.
But Argilagos said it's unfair to compare Great Providence to beers like Sam Adams, because his company's shares are more affordable and targeted at a different breed of investor.
"We're giving the little guy a chance to participate in a very exciting industry," he said. "We don't want to be a Sam Adams."
Great Providence intends to stay small, never exceeding 50,000 barrels a year, and serving only Connecticut, Rhode Island and Massachusetts, he said.
In an unorthodox move, the company is marketing its shares directly, rather than through an investment banker.
In April 1996, Great Providence gave away 10 free shares each to some 20,000 callers who responded to a radio ad campaign in Rhode Island.
"We're trying to use the Internet as a marketing tool, and for a while we were known as the wacky guys who were giving stock away," said Argilagos.

Great Providence is not the first microbrewer to use the Internet to sell stock. New York-based Spring Street Brewing Co., which makes Wit beer, launched a stock offering over the Web in 1995 and began selling it via the Internet in March 1996.
As Argilagos sees it, Great Providence already has 20,000 shareholders who will be asking for the product at local bars.
The company's first commercial batch of beer will emerge from the fermenting tanks in late January and will be served up on draft at about 20 Rhode Island locations.
A rollout in Connecticut and Massachusetts will soon follow, and Great Providence will also begin bottling its product.
It plans to serve up four varieties of brew: Pilsner, Russian Imperial Stout, India Pale Ale and a seasonal beer.
Great Providence also plans a Trappist-style, bottle-conditioned ale, as well as 100 special bottles to commemorate the July 1997 handover of Hong Kong to China.
It will be the first Rhode Island brewery since the once-proud Narragansett went under in the 1970s, Argilagos said.
